cues.text: Why is the EPR paradox weird?
Take a pair of entangled particles, and send one of them off to Alpha Centauri.
When Alice measures her particle, Bob's particle becomes known, even though Bob hasn't measured it yet.
And they claim it for sure wasn't known before Alice measured. Oh no. Before that, it was in an unknowable state.
And they're like, "That's so mysterious, right?" And I'm like, why wasn't it known all along?
Well, here's why it couldn't have been known all along. We'll explain it with three increasingly true lies.
The first lie goes like this. Alice and Bob bump a phone app that gives them each a button. Pressing it shows a zero or a one.
And the app claims that, mysteriously, they'll see the same number, even if they press the button a light-year apart.
But why couldn't the app just assign each phone the same number when they bump?
OK, fair enough. On to the second lie. Now the app has two buttons, and pressing either one removes both buttons, and shows a zero or a one.
The claim is that if they press the same button, they'll see the same number, but if they press different buttons, they'll see different numbers. Even a light-year apart!
But again, why couldn't the app assign a number to each button when they bump? The same on both phones, and a different number to each button.
Then the prediction works out no matter what they each decide to press.
OK, fine. On to the third, and nearly final, lie. Now the app has three buttons, stacked like a traffic light.
And now it claims that whatever they press, they'll get the same number, unless one person presses the top button and the other presses the bottom button. Then they'll get different numbers.
Now it really is tricky. When the phones bump, what can the app assign?
If it assigns a one to the top button, then it needs a one on the middle button too, in case one person presses top and the other presses middle.
But then it needs a one on the bottom button too, in case one presses middle and the other presses bottom.
But that's no good. Now they're all ones. What if one presses the top, and the other presses the bottom?
The only way out is for the app to send some kind of instantaneous message to the other phone, the moment someone presses a button.
But that's hard when they're a light-year apart. That's really the punch line. That's the spirit of what's weird about the EPR paradox.
But the truth is an app with three buttons where, if they press the same button, they always see the same number.
If one presses the middle, and the other presses the top or the bottom, it's not a sure thing, but there's a good chance they match: about eighty-five percent.
And if one presses the top and the other the bottom, it's a coin flip: a fifty percent chance they match.
And it turns out, an app that assigns its numbers at the bump would also be impossible.
Here's why. Look at what the app writes down at any one bump. If the top and bottom numbers are different, then the middle can't match both of them.
So every time top and bottom disagree, the middle disagrees with one of them.
Top and bottom disagree half the time, so the middle's two disagreements have to add up to at least half. That's twenty-five percent each, so the middle can match at most seventy-five percent.
But real particles match eighty-five percent. Fifteen plus fifteen is only thirty, and that can't cover fifty.
In the real experiment, the buttons are the angles of a polarizing filter: zero, twenty-two and a half, and forty-five degrees. The chance of a match is the cosine squared of the angle between them.
And experiments agree with quantum mechanics, not with the app. So the answers couldn't have been written down all along, unless the phones can talk faster than light. That's what's weird.
